"A myriad of" means an extremely large number of things — so large that counting them all feels impossible. Think of it as a stronger, more vivid, more expressive way of saying "a huge number of."

As a noun, it always appears in this fixed structure:

a myriad of + [plural noun]

For example: "A myriad of stars filled the night sky." This means: there are so many stars up there that you cannot possibly count them all.

This is the most important thing to understand about "myriad." It is not a fancy synonym for "many." The gap between "many" and "a myriad of" is the gap between a crowd and an ocean.

When you say "many," the listener imagines a large but still manageable number — maybe dozens, maybe hundreds. When you say "a myriad of," you are telling the listener: this number is so enormous, so overwhelming, that wrapping your mind around the full scale of it is nearly impossible.

Imagine standing on a beach and trying to count every grain of sand under your feet. You cannot. That feeling of impossible vastness — that is exactly what "a myriad of" captures.

Beyond sheer quantity, "a myriad of" very often carries a second meaning: the things being described are not just numerous, but also diverse and varied. They come in many different forms, types, or kinds.

Consider this sentence: "The city offers a myriad of experiences."

This does not just mean the city has a lot of experiences. It means the city has an overwhelming number of different kinds of experiences — food, art, music, nightlife, history, architecture, culture — so many and so varied that you could spend a lifetime exploring them and still not exhaust them all.

So when you use "a myriad of," you are often quietly saying two things at once: there are an overwhelming number of these things, and they are wonderfully varied.

"Myriad" is a formal, literary word. You are far more likely to encounter it in books, essays, journalism, and polished speeches than in casual everyday conversation. Using it in speech is perfectly correct, but it carries a sophisticated, elevated quality. It is the kind of word a writer reaches for when they want to paint a picture of rich abundance, not merely state a number.

Compare these two sentences:

  • "There are many reasons to try this approach."
  • "There are a myriad of reasons to try this approach."

Both sentences are grammatically correct and mean roughly the same thing. But the second one feels bigger, richer, and more emphatic. It signals to the reader: the reasons are not just numerous, they are overwhelming in their abundance.

It does not mean "several." Several is a small number — five, six, seven. Myriad is always the opposite of small.

It does not require a precise count. The entire beauty of the word is that it is deliberately vague about the exact number. The point is that the quantity is beyond easy reckoning.

It does not mean "infinite." Infinite means without any end whatsoever. A myriad of things is an extremely large number — vast and overwhelming, yes — but not necessarily limitless. A myriad of grains of sand is not the same as an infinite number of grains of sand.

Whenever you encounter "a myriad of," or want to use it yourself, let this be your mental anchor:

"There are so many of these things — countless in number, rich in variety, and overwhelming in their totality — that no list could capture them all."

A few more examples to solidify it:

  • "Scientists have discovered a myriad of new species in the deep ocean." → So many new species, in so many different forms, that cataloguing them is an enormous challenge.
  • "She faced a myriad of challenges in her first year abroad." → Not just a few difficulties, but an avalanche of them — language barriers, homesickness, financial stress, cultural adjustment, and so much more.
  • "The museum houses a myriad of ancient artifacts." → An overwhelming, diverse collection spanning civilizations, centuries, and continents.

In each case, "a myriad of" does more than a number ever could. It does not tell you how many — it tells you the number is beyond easy telling, and that richness and variety come with it.
